data.title: GOP House member on 'embarrassing' SC prospects: 'Darline is dragging Rs'
data.description:
A House Republican called the competitive Senate race in South Carolina “embarrassing,” adding that incumbent Sen. Darline Graham (R) is “dragging Rs down the ticket.”

“Republicans won this seat by 18 points. The fact it’s this close and the speaker has to come to SC 1 to drag the R across the finish line is embarrassing,” the anonymous member wrote in an exchange posted Thursday by NewsNation senior congressional correspondent Joe Khalil on the social platform X.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is expected to campaign in South Carolina’s 1st Congressional District, according to local news station WCSC.

A tight Senate race is unfolding in South Carolina between Graham and her Democratic opponent Annie Andrews. Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) leans in favor of Graham, giving her a 65 percent chance of winning the race.

However, a recent a New York Times/Siena University poll showed both candidates with 48 percent support among likely voters in South Carolina, a state which has not elected a Democrat to the upper chamber of Congress since 1998.

“Darline is dragging Rs down the ticket” the Republican member wrote, as recounted in Khalil’s post. “The only saving grace is that the governors race is where it should be.”

President Trump recently made his third and final trip to South Carolina to boost support for Graham’s Senate bid. Graham was appointed to the seat by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster (R) following the death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R).

In the state’s gubernatorial race, South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson (R) has a 74 percent chance of winning against his Democratic opponent Jermaine Johnson, according to DDHQ.

data.title: Ro Khanna and the fight for the post-Bernie left
data.description:
“Stop shilling for billionaires,” Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) said of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, as we strolled across the University of California, Berkeley’s campus. Silicon Valley’s congressman has made the rebuke something of a refrain. The two have taken opposing sides on Proposition 40, the billionaire tax now buckling under an onslaught of money from tech billionaires.

You wouldn’t have guessed its troubles from the mood at the rally on campus last week. There, a budding California resistance gathered around candidates, including Rep. Aisha Wahab (D); Jane Kim, who is running for insurance commissioner; and Angela Gonzales-Torres who is running against Democratic Rep. Jimmy Gomez, all backed by the Working Families Party.

Khanna was asked the obvious question: “Will you run for president?” The crowd roared. A couple of “Ro for President” signs supplied their own answer. It was hard to imagine another California politician being greeted quite like this at Berkeley, as king hereafter. Progressive capitalism was the cause, and the crowd had settled on its leader.

Khanna finds it easy to define himself against Newsom. Newsom is a neoliberal. Khanna is a “New Deal Democrat” who’ll tax the oligarchs. Newsom triangulates on Gaza. Khanna opposes military aid to Israel, period.

Yet in the 2028 Democratic primary, his most direct interfactional rival may lie elsewhere. Newsom would compete with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D). For Khanna, the contest for the left would more likely run through socialist Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) — if they both run, at least.

I asked Khanna what, in practice, distinguishes progressive capitalism from socialism. “Free enterprise means that the government doesn’t have control over all of the means of production,” he said. “You wouldn’t want Donald Trump controlling everything.”

Fair enough. What he wants, he said, is a system that works for “hardworking individuals,” rather than people “accumulating wealth in their sleep because of the growth of the stock market.” His answer became a critique of capitalism as currently practiced. The distinction remained elusive.

I tried again. What would he actually do differently from Ocasio-Cortez or Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.)? Khanna pointed to a capital fund supporting entrepreneurship, innovation and small businesses, and to the jobs and entrepreneurship programs he had been setting up across America.

So is the difference a matter of priorities?

“A New Deal,” he said.

Khanna is, so far, doing reasonably well at the delicate business of remaining credible on the left while admitting to being a capitalist. As socialism gains ground in the party, that takes a certain suppleness. He represents Silicon Valley, so it’s not really his fault — wink, wink.

His offer to the left has its attractions: He won’t throw the socialists under the bus when, say, Bill Maher invites him on his show. He certainly didn’t in his conversation with me. I asked about the legacy of Woke 1.0 — the 2020-era peak of defund-the-police slogans and critical race theory. In August, Ocasio-Cortez had laughed the period off with a line borrowed from a Brooklyn councilman: “Woke one was crazy.” Had Democrats seriously reckoned with the era’s excesses, I asked, or merely learned to shrug them away? What did they owe voters?

“I’ve always had a deep love of this country,” he said. “I think we need to celebrate America’s history and culture.”

He went on to invoke slavery and Jim Crow. “Woke means being aware of injustices — I think there’s nothing wrong with that.” The answer offered little reckoning, but plenty of reassurance. His endorsement of socialist Francesca Hong (D) in her unsuccessful Wisconsin gubernatorial primary bid might have earned him some trust among the Democratic Socialists of America faithful, too. Her pandemic-era statements against the police and Thanksgiving became a political liability, but Khanna stood by her side anyway.

Meanwhile, his willingness to celebrate America’s history, defend strong borders and accept the need for an immigration enforcement agency gives moderate Democrats something to like. Khanna seems determined to keep everyone in the conversation.

Khanna knows the guts of the world he proposes to reform and has a silver tongue for soothing those whose feathers he ruffles. His resume offers some explanation: a stint as President Obama’s deputy assistant secretary of Commerce, followed by work as an intellectual-property lawyer at techy law firm Wilson Sonsini.

When Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in 2023, Khanna went all-in supporting a federal guarantee of its depositors’ money. There was a progressive case for intervention: businesses needed to meet payroll, and allowing regional banks to fail would concentrate still more power in the largest banks. He made it fluently. There was also an obvious constituency interest. When Silicon Valley needed Washington, its congressman answered the call.

That combination of appeals could make Khanna more than another Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.). Khanna is betting 2028 will be no 2020 — that a left tired of losing will tolerate a candidate who can win over the Democratic Socialists of America organizat and Curt Mills of the American Conservative, who has suggested that he’d take Khanna over Secretary of State Marco Rubio (R).

Khanna has already earned some goodwill across those constituencies. Yet Ocasio-Cortez, heir to Sanders’s movement, has never had to explain what separates her from socialism. Khanna does.

For now, he has room to keep making his case to all of them.

William Liang is a writer living in San Francisco. He volunteers for Connie Chan’s congressional campaign in California’s 11th District.

data.title: Stevens to appear alongside El-Sayed for first time, but expects apology
data.description:
Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) will appear alongside Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed for the first time this Sunday in what appears to be a reluctant show of unity after criticizing the Democratic nominee for his comments about Israel.

Stevens confirmed Friday in a statement posted to the social platform X that she would join Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.) and El-Sayed at a church service in Detroit this Sunday.

“I say this with no race to run and nothing to gain,” Stevens said. “The Jewish and African American communities of my district deserve to see their leaders show up for them rather than fight over them.”

A spokesperson for El-Sayed’s campaign did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment about the joint appearance or Stevens’s comments.

Stevens said she accepted the invitation to appear alongside El-Sayed from Clyburn, not from El-Sayed’s campaign.

The joint appearance comes after Stevens’s fiancé revealed he would vote for El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, because of El-Sayed’s rhetoric about Israel.

Tension emerged over a digital ad run by an outside progressive group, in which a woman is grocery shopping and appears to blame Israel for high prices. El-Sayed’s campaign previously said they were not responsible for the ad.

Stevens criticized the ad for “fearmongering” and told CNN Wednesday that a lot of Michigan voters are “hurt” and “confused,” calling on El-Sayed to denounce the ad.

In her statement Friday, she again criticized her former primary opponent for not condemning the ad more forcefully, calling on the Democratic nominee to get “Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.”

“The ad did not invent its argument; it dramatized one Dr. El-Sayed has made in his own words throughout this campaign: that Israel is the reason Michigan cannot afford schools, healthcare, and child care,” Stevens said. “I therefore expect him to apologize for those statements as well.”

El-Sayed has been highly critical of Israel throughout the campaign, with AIPAC, a pro-Israel lobbying group, spending millions on behalf of Stevens in the primary. El-Sayed ultimately defeated Stevens by a narrow margin.

Rogers has repeatedly attacked El-Sayed for his comments about Israel and is courting disaffected Jewish voters, including Democrats. Polls show a competitive race, but one which El-Sayed narrowly leads.

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, gives El-Sayed a 73 percent chance to retain the seat for Democrats.

data.title: How 'You Can See Everything' unmasks our modern age of manufactured reality
data.description:
Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder’s “You Can See Everything” is a movie for our times — not only because it is the rare documentary with box office appeal and Oscar buzz, but because it strikes at something in the culture of this century that almost defies description. 

The film centers on the Theranos debacle of the last decade and how someone like Elizabeth Holmes tries to repair a private and public life after being classified as one of the business world’s biggest frauds. But in a larger sense, it is also about the gnawing unease and increasing difficulty we are all experiencing in our own lives as we contend with today’s grift economy, in a world of diffuse media, algorithmic filter bubbles and infinite forums for people to speak their version of the truth.  

“You Can See Everything” also homes in on the prized ethos of “fake it ‘til you make it” that now defines business and startup culture. Holmes was one of the most flagrant Steve Jobs clones, right up to the turtleneck, applying her brand of magical thinking to blood testing the way others did to apps or digital currencies or virtual worlds or artificial intelligence. 

But what happens when such magical thinking extends to fraud, billions’ worth of investment, and the corruption of medicine, a field whose very foundation is “do no harm?” Or when your belief that a piece of technology might be able to deliver someday on what you are promising is not the same as actually being able to deliver today? 

Yet Oppenheim and Fielder have no interest in a deep dive on the details of Theranos, as multiple news investigations, television shows and court proceedings already have undertaken. It is enough to have the movie turn on a single statement Holmes made to The New York Times in 2023, unlocking a heuristic for what might be fundamental dishonesty or fundamental confusion, as Fielder deploys a lethal narrowing of eyes and the most skeptical “OK” this side of Larry David.  

Perhaps that figured into the calculus of Holmes to bring Fielder and Oppenheim into this sort of project in the first place. By limiting this embedded recording to a few weeks in a San Diego guest house, it might have been possible for Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, to play-act the image they wanted to create in the weeks leading up to Holmes’s incarceration. It’s essentially what some brands have been doing for decades in trying to shift the narrative — maybe we can call this docu-washing. 

There is so much strangeness to what we see, though, that it is difficult to fathom what that attempt at manipulating image and discourse might have been.  

Is Holmes really just a naif who might be on the spectrum and suffering from the PTSD of a sexual assault at Stanford, as well as the victim of a Svengali-like manipulation by the men in her life?  

Is Billy really losing his grip on reality because of what has happened to Holmes, or is it one more con designed to solicit money, sympathy or something else? Are his strong feelings for Charlie Kirk a result of red-pilling and being chronically online during Holmes’s incarceration, or is he cynically building a framework for a pardon from a pro-Kirk president? 

Are they both two very confused people still in love and trying to build a family, or are they just deeply embedded in characters they agreed to create for Holmes’s post-Theranos life?   

Even amid the fascinating mystery swirling around Holmes and Evans, the second half of the film does not hesitate to interrogate post-Holmes media like “The Dropout,” which seems to have created its own version of reality “based on a true story.” Here, the focus turns to the media that did create a new Holmes character, cutting its own corners of the truth in an attempt to create a more compelling emotional reality. 

Dramatic license is not medical malpractice, but when dealing with real people, it can also be its own form of bad faith. The great power of this film is that it does not just put Holmes, Evans and the associated grift economy under the microscope, but the grift economy’s outrage machine as well — and even the makers of the movie itself. 

We can see everything in “You Can See Everything,” but seeing is not the same as knowing. Fielder and Oppenheim’s film is so effective because it knows that too. 

Ian Chaffee is a technology and startup media relations consultant based in Los Angeles.

data.title: DOJ accuses Peltola, Democrats of misleading a federal court
data.description:
The Justice Department on Thursday accused Mary Peltola of misleading a federal court in the latest filing in their lawsuit seeking to block certification of the Alaska Senate election.

“Apparently emboldened by the success of their reported plot to deceive Alaskan voters, Alaskans For Mary and the DSCC appear to have turned to misleading this Court,” the amended complaint filed Thursday read.

“They orchestrated this sham campaign for the purpose of misleading Alaskan voters and getting Peltola elected,” it added.

The DOJ’s lawsuit, initially filed last week, argues that the U.S. Senate election in Alaska will be invalid unless incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) wins due to voter confusion about a candidate with the same name also appearing on the ballot.

The latest filing cites The New York Times recently reported that Peltola’s campaign was directly involved in recruiting someone with the same name as her opponent, Sen. Dan Sullivan (R).

“Although what the New York Times reports is not always true, its reporting here aligns with what the United States has been alleging on information and belief,” the filing read. “It also aligns with common sense.”

Even if Peltola’s campaign did indeed recruit Dan J. Sullivan, that action would not be against the law, Scott Kendall, an Alaska lawyer and former GOP operative, told The Hill.

“These allegations don’t make the Department of Justice’s case a better case,” Kendall said. “There’s no basis for this lawsuit.”

Kendall said ballot-stacking “can be a nasty, dirty trick” and “there can be bad motives behind it, but according to our Alaska Supreme Court, which is empowered to interpret Alaska law, it is not illegal.”

The DOJ has also issued dozens of subpoenas in connection with the case which have been sent to Peltola’s Senate campaign offices as well as the offices of Dan J. Sullivan.

Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R), on Wednesday, ordered an investigation into whether Peltola’s campaign violated state law in the alleged scheme. The House Oversight and Government Reform Committee also launched an investigation into the former Democratic lawmaker.

In a Truth Social post on Wednesday, President Trump said Peltola should face legal and political consequences. He has also said Peltola should not be allowed to run for Senate after the allegations.

Peltola, on Thursday, denied any knowledge of the alleged ballot-stacking scheme, saying she “knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent.”

Her campaign has also denied any involvement in the matter.

The competitive race in Alaska leans narrowly in favor of the Democrat, whom nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ  gives 60 percent chance of winning.

data.title: North Korea linked to $6.3B Binance hack
data.description:
A North Korea-based cybercrime group appears to be behind a $6.3 billion hack of the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, according to two blockchain intelligence firms.

Both TRM Labs and Chainalysis tied the largest crypto hack on record to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking unit that has previously targeted the digital asset industry.

Billions of dollars’ worth of crypto began moving out of Binance wallets on Thursday afternoon. The company quickly suspended all deposits and withdrawals, and crypto firms froze about $3 billion in assets tied to the incident.

The attacker moved approximately $6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on XRP Ledger, Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron, Solana and several other blockchain networks, with much of this occurring over the span of around 20 minutes, according to TRM Labs.

While the industry managed to freeze a significant portion of assets, the attacker still controls $2.4 billion “beyond any issuer’s reach,” the blockchain intelligence firm noted.

Chainalysis underscored that once the hack began, the attacker was “in a race against the clock” to swap out freezable assets, like USDT and USDC stablecoins, for non-freezable assets, like Bitcoin and Ethereum.

“It was only a matter of time before the issuers of those stablecoins would freeze those funds,” it said.

Several aspects of the Binance hack match earlier North Korea-linked incidents, including the $1.5 billion hack of the crypto exchange Bybit last year, TRM Labs noted.

Binance has vowed to cover all losses associated with the incident. It said Friday morning that it has reserved more than $6.34 billion in company funds for this effort.

“Difficult times like this are a great reminder of how strong our industry is when we work together,” Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said in a video posted to social platform X. “We are grateful to our partners that acted quickly to freeze their assets, to global law enforcement who we are working with hand-in-hand to seek justice.”

“But most of all, we are grateful to our users for their patience and understanding,” he continued. “Rest assured that we are working nonstop to resolve this, to make the users whole and live up to their trust.”

data.title: New federal rule requires drug middlemen to disclose how they're paid
data.description:
The companies that manage billions of dollars in prescription drug spending for employers and workers will soon be required to inform their clients all the different ways they get paid under a new rule released by the Trump administration Thursday. 

A final rule by the Department of Labor (DOL) will require pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) for the first time to disclose detailed information about all their fees and compensation from drug manufacturers, pharmacies, consultants and more — which could help shed light on potential conflicts of interest.  

PBM compensation has long been shrouded in secrecy and confidential agreements. The Labor Department said the new transparency could help employers negotiate contracts and seek lower prescription drug costs. 

“This is a win for every American worker who has ever paid too much at the pharmacy counter,” Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said in a statement. “For years, PBMs have operated in the shadows, pocketing hidden fees while workers and employers were left in the dark. Today, President Trump is delivering the transparency Americans deserve – and putting American workers first.”  

High prescription drug costs are a major concern to voters this election cycle, and the Trump administration has been promoting price transparency to reduce costs, though with minimal practical impact. 

The final PBM rule is projected to save health plans and enrollees more than $800 million annually due to reduced prescription prices, the Department of Health and Human Services said. At most, the rule could save up to $22 billion over 10 years. 

Still, transparency advocates and employer groups applauded. 

“Large employers pay for their workers’ prescriptions, but many can’t see how much of that money their PBM and any affiliated entity keeps,” James Gelfand, president and CEO of the ERISA Industry Committee, said in a statement. “This rule changes that. Employers will be able to check the numbers, ask hard questions, and hold their vendors accountable to the contract.” 

Pharmacy benefit managers are the intermediaries in the prescription drug supply chain who negotiate discounts with drug companies, paying pharmacies and determining which drugs patients can access and how much they cost.  

They are often owned by and integrated into large insurance companies. The three biggest PBMs are UnitedHealth Group’s Optum Rx, CVS Health’s Caremark and Cigna’s Express Scripts, which represent about 80 percent of all U.S. prescriptions. 

The rule will apply to self-insured employers, typically larger businesses that pay their own health claims. Implementation will begin on July 1, 2027. The rule enacts severe financial penalties and potential invalidation of the PBM contract if the companies don’t cooperate. 

The PBM industry faced intense scrutiny on Capitol Hill last year; essentially every committee in both chambers with jurisdiction over healthcare drafted PBM reform legislation, and Trump also frequently railed against them. 

Congress passed a law earlier this year to require PBMs to disclose more information. Officials said the law guided the drafting of the rule, with parts of the law to take effect after the rule does. 

Critics say PBMs profit by steering people to more expensive drugs, driving up overall healthcare spending. 

The rule was initially proposed in January and faced significant opposition from PBMs, health insurers and even some pharmaceutical companies.  

David Marin, president and CEO of the PBM industry group Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, said the DOL rule is “redundant” because Congress already enacted PBM transparency reform and called it “regulatory overreach” beyond the intent of Congress.   

“[W]e are extremely concerned that it will lead to higher patient costs and less competition, the opposite of the Department’s stated intent,” Marin said in a statement. “Patients, employers, and unions will have no new meaningful transparency from this action, but prescription drug benefits will now be more expensive.”

data.title: The US should strongly advocate for political prisoner releases, global freedom
data.description:
It is a familiar picture. An emaciated political prisoner walks off a plane, greeted by family and strangers stunned to see this person in the flesh. On the former captive’s face flash emotions of both incomprehensible relief and dizzying disbelief. These rare releases of political prisoners typically follow the tireless advocacy of family, friends, governments, and civil society.

As we celebrate these breakthrough moments of freedom, we should never forget the bigger picture that lurks behind each release, namely brutal autocratic regimes consolidating and asserting power by using human pawns and the capricious denial of freedom.

The United States should continue to advocate for the release of political prisoners, utilize tools to punish and deter such abuses, and — most importantly — recognize that any regime involved in political imprisonment lacks the values and trustworthiness for long-term American partnership.

We must naturally pursue short-term engagement with many nations to advance and protect American interests. We should also acknowledge, however, that the depravity of a regime denying freedom to its own citizens undermines that nation’s viability as a trusted partner. Those nations that share our democratic values are stronger, better, more sustainable partners.

We have celebrated the rare prisoner releases by name. Journalist Jason Rezian, freed from Iran. Pastor Ezra Jin, freed from China. Journalist Evan Gershkovich, freed from Russia. Activist Maryam Akbari Monfared, freed from Iran. Artist-turned-activist Luis Manuel Otero Alcantara, freed from Cuba. Pastor-turned-activist Evan Mawarire, freed from Zimbabwe.

Each release is unquestionably a welcome development, and at the George W. Bush Institute, we celebrate every individual who is restored to freedom. Yet each is a reminder of a growing tide of autocratic leaders, often loosely aligned with each other, willing to throw countless numbers of innocent people in prison, most often for practicing their faith, writing a news article, advocating for their rights, or demanding justice.

These autocratic leaders direct myriad government staff — from senior officials to the lowest prison guard — to deny these people their freedom, to harass their families and limit contact, to treat them with disdain and abuse, to deny access to medicine, adequate food, and fresh air, and — all too often — to subject them to inhuman abuse and torture. These are usually strategic, planned arrests designed not only to silence the individual but to send chills through the entire community.

All of this is because these individuals dared to worship, speak, assemble and associate, foundational freedoms we know well — and value deeply — in the United States.

Quite often, these regimes follow high-profile releases with the arrest of other activists or colleagues of the released person, a “replenishment” of political prisoners. And frequently they continue to harass the individual and their community long after the release has occurred. All too often, these individuals are forced from their home country permanently.

Each release is simply undoing a deeply unjust action that these rulers chose to do; it should be recognized as such, not as an act of charity.

Since Jin’s July release, at least seven Christian house churches have been raided. At least 150 pastors remain imprisoned, and eight Christians who were seized with Jin remain behind bars.

Since Otero Alcantara’s July release, at least a dozen more people have been incarcerated, according to Prisoners Defenders, a leading group tracking political imprisonment in Cuba. It estimates that Cuban jails held 1,339 political prisoners as of August, a number that has steadily increased over the course of the year.

The administration and members of Congress should expand their efforts to call for the release of political prisoners, especially those held by China, Russia, Iran and North Korea, authoritarian nations increasingly aligned in their interests.

American elected officials should continue to call for the release of individual prisoners by name: Wang Yi, Jimmy Lai, and Dr. Gulshan Abbas in China; Lev Schosberg in Russia; Narges Mohammadi in Iran.

This will serve as a powerful reminder that the U.S. stands for liberty and won’t turn a blind eye to repression by these regimes. It would also be an important boost for democracy defenders in each country, showing that they are not alone and that the democratic world stands with them.

Beyond individual case advocacy, the administration and U.S. Congress should use the powerful tools at their disposal, including sanctions under the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act, to impose a real penalty on those involved with imprisoning innocent democracy activists.

Finally, the administration and Congress should calibrate relations accordingly with all nations that choose to use political imprisonment to silence freedom defenders.

Each person reunited with their loved ones is a reason to rejoice. But let us honor their stories, struggles and aspirations by focusing on the bigger fight against autocratic regimes and to show them that we won’t allow the normalization of their dehumanizing practice of political imprisonment.

Nicole Bibbins Sedaca is the Kelly and David Pfeil Fellow at the George W. Bush Institute.

data.title: Leo XIV becomes first pope ever to vote in US general election
data.description:
VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope to vote in a U.S. general election.

The Vatican confirmed Friday that the Chicago-born pontiff submitted a mail-in ballot in Chicago ahead of next week’s midterm elections, citing his long-standing belief in civic participation.

Leo, formerly Robert Prevost, “has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen” and has done so “whenever he was eligible to do so,” the Holy See press office said.

The statement said he had also voted while living in Peru whenever he was eligible.

“The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes,” it added.

Leo’s vote was first reported by the Chicago Sun-Times, which quoted the chief of staff at the Will County clerk’s office as saying the pope, registered at a New Lenox address, requested a mail-in ballot on Oct. 3.

It is unclear how Leo returned the ballot. His brother, John Prevost, was in Rome this week accompanying parishioners from St. Jude’s, an Augustinian-run parish in New Lenox, Ill. The elder Prevost attends Mass there, and Leo gave a talk at the parish in 2024 while still a cardinal.

Since 2000, Robert Prevost has voted in five primary elections, requesting Democratic ballots twice and Republican ballots three times, according to records held by the Illinois State Board of Elections.

The records do not show which candidates he supported. Illinois voters must declare a party preference to receive a ballot in a primary, when parties choose their nominees for the general election. No such declaration is required in general elections.

While registered in heavily Democratic Cook County, Prevost requested Democratic primary ballots in 2008 and 2010. After moving to the more conservative suburban Will County, he requested Republican primary ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016.

The records also show that he submitted ballots in every general election since 2000 except those in 2020 and 2022.

data.title: Drone warfare will be won at the operator level
data.description:
We are witnessing modern warfare create a paradox. The battlefield has never had more intelligence, yet the soldier may have less time than ever to use it. A drone can be detected by one system, classified by another, tracked by a third and defeated by yet another. Each system may work as designed. But if those capabilities can’t converge around the person who has seconds to act, technological superiority becomes irrelevant.

It poses a fundamental and lethal gap for our warfighters.

Drone warfare will be won at the operator level. The advantage won’t belong to the military with the best drones or the most sophisticated interceptor, but to the military that brings intelligence and capability together around the individual solider, creating a decision advantage at machine speed.

For decades, military modernization has delivered extraordinary advances in sensing, communications and precision. But drone warfare exposes a dangerous weakness. A small aerial threat can emerge with little warning, leaving a soldier seconds to understand what’s happening and respond. The challenge isn’t simply whether information exists. It’s whether the person who needs it can understand it and act before it’s too late.

Information superiority doesn’t automatically translate into decision superiority. A warfighter surrounded by sensors and intelligence may still lack a clear picture of what to do next. More information can become a burden when every new capability introduces another stream of data demanding attention.

We have spent years putting more information in front of soldiers. Now we must remove the complexity. Militaries are developing increasingly capable electronic warfare systems. The challenge is making them work together.

Rather than building systems around individual platforms and asking operators to navigate between them, we should build around the operator — something like an Iron Dome for the individual. Sensors, autonomous assets and defensive capabilities should converge through a common coordination layer that absorbs technical complexity and presents the operator with a clear understanding of the threat and available options.

Agentic artificial intelligence could transform this process. Unlike AI that simply analyzes information, agentic systems can coordinate tasks and available tools. Such a system could process sensor data, classify a threat, identify available defensive capabilities and present options. The operator would no longer need to navigate multiple systems to understand what can be done.

The goal isn’t to show warfighters everything a machine knows. It’s to provide what they need to know when they need it. Machine speed should compress complexity while humans remain in charge.

Our perspectives come from different experiences. One of us spent two decades in Army Special Operations, including 18 combat deployments. Another has worked across government and emerging technology, focusing on artificial intelligence and systems design. And one of us investigated and uncovered dangerous flaws on the production line of one of the nation’s most complicated and important military aircraft. 

Yet all these experiences point to the same principle: Battlefield technology should make the operator more capable, not irrelevant.

Such a system could give an individual soldier a tactical edge by coordinating capabilities that once required multiple interfaces or specialists. This wouldn’t eliminate command structures. It would create greater situational awareness and improve decision-making on the battlefield.

But it must work under battlefield conditions even when communications fail, GPS degrades and networks go down. Adversaries can manipulate information and attack the systems carrying it. Battlefield AI must be designed for degraded environments, enabling useful intelligence even when distant command centers or cloud connections are unavailable.

The Pentagon should also expand how it measures counter-drone performance. Detection range, interception probability, accuracy and cost remain important. But so does the time between detecting a threat and enabling a human response. A system that detects a drone earlier but complicates the decision-making process isn’t an operational advantage.

There are real risks. AI can misclassify threats, fail in unexpected conditions or encourage excessive trust in machine recommendations. These dangers are serious when lethal force is involved. The answer is not simply greater autonomy.

Human oversight must be built in. Operators need more than the ability to approve a final action; they need situational understanding and authority over decisions. AI should perform tasks that machines can execute faster while helping humans make better decisions under pressure.

The U.S. must stop asking only how much more technology it can put in warfighters’ hands. It must ask how much complexity it can remove. As drones proliferate and autonomy increases, the time available to make decisions shrinks. More sensors and interceptors won’t matter if operators can’t act quickly.

Drone warfare will be won by the military that connects its systems, compresses decision time and puts intelligence where it matters most: with the person whose life depends on it.

The goal of battlefield AI is not to remove the human from the fight. It is to give the human an advantage within it.

Thomas Payne is a recipient of the U.S. Army’s Medal of Honor for actions during his service in Iraq in 2015. Cesar R. Hernandez is a fellow at Harvard’s Kennedy School of Government, a developer at the MIT Media Lab, and an MBA graduate of Oxford University. Alan M. Cohn is a Peabody and Emmy Award-winning journalist.
